scenario_analysis.executive_summary: The July 9 drone survey shows moderate to high disease pressure across the 9‑zone rice/wheat field in Korba, with a mean health score of 0.55 and 70% stress. Hotspot zones Z05, Z06 and Z08 exhibit elevated severity indices and spread risk, driven by recent heavy rain, high humidity and leaf‑wetness conditions. Coldspot zones Z03, Z04 and Z09 remain comparatively healthier, likely due to micro‑climatic shelter and better drainage. Immediate integrated management is required to curb further epidemic expansion.

hotspots_analysis.why_hotspots_formed: Zones Z05, Z06 and Z08 became hotspots because the capture day recorded 8.1 mm rain and the preceding week accumulated 144 mm, creating prolonged leaf wetness (high_leaf_wetness_risk=True). The prevailing wind (max 16.1 km/h) aligned with the field’s gentle slope, channeling spores from adjacent infected zones (high Gi* values for Z05 and Z06). Unsupervised detection flagged a dominance of LeafSpot_Brown (58 detections) and General_Lesion lesions, both favoured by temperatures near 30 °C and relative humidity above 85 %. The combination of high humidity, recent rainfall, and spatial adjacency amplified inoculum build‑up and dispersal, producing moderate to high hotspot classifications.

hotspot_zones_details.environmental_driver: high leaf wetness from recent rain

spread_mechanisms: Wind‑borne spore transport amplified by 16 km/h gusts
Rain splash and surface runoff distributing inoculum across adjacent grids

coldspots_analysis.why_not_affected: Coldspot zones Z03, Z04 and Z09 experienced slightly lower leaf‑wetness periods due to micro‑topographic depressions that promote faster drainage, and they are positioned on the leeward side of the prevailing wind, reducing spore influx. Additionally, the recent fungicide application on the western field edge likely protected these areas, and the crop variety in these grids shows partial tolerance to chlorosis.
coldspots_analysis.protective_lessons: Effective drainage, wind sheltering and timely fungicide coverage can suppress disease build‑up; replicating these practices (e.g., contour bunds, windbreaks, and staggered spray schedules) across the field will help lower overall risk.

environmental_inferences.temperature_effect: Daytime maxima around 30 °C approach the optimal range for many foliar pathogens, accelerating lesion expansion.
environmental_inferences.humidity_leaf_wetness_effect: Mean RH of 85 % and max 98 % sustain leaf wetness >12 h, a key driver for both leaf‑spot and chlorosis development.
environmental_inferences.rainfall_effect_7d: 144 mm in the prior week created a moist canopy and soil surface, enhancing spore germination and splash dispersal.
environmental_inferences.wind_dispersal_risk: Maximum wind of 16 km/h is sufficient to carry lightweight urediniospores across zones, especially from high‑Gi* hotspots.
environmental_inferences.soil_moisture_inference: Excessive rainfall likely raised soil moisture to near saturation, promoting chlorosis and reducing root oxygen availability.

risk_inferences.short_term_72h_risk: High – hotspots Z05 and Z06 may spread to adjacent neutral zones via wind‑borne spores and rain splash within the next three days.
risk_inferences.medium_term_2week_risk: Moderate – unless fungicide interventions are applied, disease pressure could expand to all neutral zones, raising overall field stress above 80 %.
risk_inferences.yield_risk_assessment: Potential 12‑18 % yield loss if hotspots are not managed, driven by leaf area reduction from leaf‑spot lesions and chlorosis‑induced photosynthetic decline.

priority_1_immediate_24h: Apply a broad‑spectrum protectant (e.g., a mixed mode of action containing a triazole + strobilurin) at 0.2 L ha⁻¹ to zones Z05, Z06 and Z08
Conduct targeted foliar spray of a copper‑based product to neutral zones Z01 and Z02 to curb early spread
priority_2_shortterm_1_3d: Implement a rain‑fastening adjuvant to improve spray retention
Increase canopy airflow by low‑height mechanical windbreak removal in zones Z03 and Z04
priority_3_mediumterm_1_2wk: Schedule a second fungicide application with a different FRAC group to prevent resistance buildup
Introduce bio‑fungicide (Bacillus subtilis) seed‑ling drench in all zones

High‑dose strobilurin + adjuvant at 0.25 L ha⁻¹; monitor for leaf scorch
Copper‑based protectant at 0.15 L ha⁻¹; add foliar nitrogen boost
No chemical needed; focus on drainage improvement
Maintain current regime; consider windbreak reinforcement
Confirm fungicide residual activity; if needed, apply a systemic protectant

cultural_practices: Create shallow contour ridges to enhance runoff
Plant windbreak rows on the upwind side of the field
Adjust planting density to improve airflow
mitigation_plan.chemical_fungicide_program: Rotate between a triazole (FRAC 3) and a strobilurin (FRAC 11) for protectant applications, followed by a multi‑site protectant (e.g., a copper or mancozeb) for residual control; avoid consecutive use of the same FRAC group.
biological_options: Bacillus subtilis strain for foliar spray
irrigation_nutrition_adjustments: Reduce late‑season irrigation to prevent prolonged leaf wetness
Apply foliar potassium (0.5 % K₂SO₄) to mitigate chlorosis
mitigation_plan.followup_surveillance_schedule: Conduct drone re‑scans every 5 days for the next 2 weeks, complemented by ground scouting of hotspot edges within 24 h of each flight

scenario_analysis.confidence_notes: The pathogen detections are derived from an unsupervised image model without ground‑truth validation, so class assignments (LeafSpot_Brown, General_Lesion, Chlorosis_Yellow) may contain false positives. Weather inputs are based on a single station and may not capture micro‑climate variability across the 3 × 3 grid. Recommendations assume standard rice/wheat phenology for mid‑July in Chhattisgarh; local cultivar specifics could modify disease susceptibility.
